SMTO-HTTP-0079 — The service tried to send SMTO to a different site

GUID: fe74ca33-590d-44cd-9b5d-4601c90a5cee
Slug: http-redirect-blocked
Domain: HTTP · Subsystem: http

What happened

  • The service answered by pointing SMTO to another address. SMTO didn't follow it, so your sign-in details weren't passed to a site this connection doesn't trust.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. In the conversation, ask SMTO which address the service tried to send it to. Knowing the new address tells you whether the service simply moved or something is wrong.
  2. If it is the service's correct new address, open Parameter Store, select the connection, change Base URL to that address, save, and select Test connection. Requests sent straight to the right address don't get redirected, and the sign-in stays with the site it belongs to.
  3. If the request was meant to change something, check in the service whether that change already happened before asking SMTO to try again. The service received the first request before it answered with the redirect.

What success looks like

  • Requests go straight to the service's address and come back with a reply, without being redirected.

If it still fails

  • If you don't recognize the address, don't point the connection at it. Send the copied error details to the person who runs the service.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The HTTP client blocked a followed redirect because its Location was invalid or left the original origin while authentication, secret headers, cookies or a bound connection were present.

What this means

  • A followed redirect has an invalid URL or would cross the original origin while authentication, secret headers, cookies or a bound connection are present. The specific receipt owns dispatch and effect truth. Authentication exchanges, resource requests and Gateway admission are separate phases; rendering this explanation performs no request and never authorizes replay of an uncertain mutation.

Why this can happen

  • A followed redirect has an invalid URL or would cross the original origin while authentication, secret headers, cookies or a bound connection are present.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect sanitized Location/origin and redirect history; an explicit origin allowlist does not authorize credential forwarding on redirects.

How to fix it

  • _execute_http_request blocks a 3xx whose Location is invalid or crosses origin when credentials, secret headers, cookies or a bound connection are present; allowed_origins does not authorize credential redirects. Inspect the Location header and send the request directly to the intended final origin (update base_url if the service moved); never forward credentials to an untrusted host.
  • Inspect the response location and intended endpoint. Use an explicitly permitted destination without forwarding credentials to an untrusted host.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The intended endpoint is reached through permitted routing without crossing the protected redirect boundary.

What not to do

  • Do not silently substitute a different target for a saved run or move its existing execution authority.

Technical notes

  • The specific receipt owns dispatch and effect truth. Authentication exchanges, resource requests and Gateway admission are separate phases; rendering this explanation performs no request and never authorizes replay of an uncertain mutation.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
